newsitem.title: USA: IFC sees heady growth rate slowing this year.
newsitem.headline: IFC sees heady growth rate slowing this year.

text.p: The World Bank arm that supports private enterprise said Thursday its help for developing countries is strongly in demand, although other investors were increasingly picking up part of the load.
The International Finance Corp. said total financing in the year ended June 30 hit a record $3.2 billion, up from $2.9 billion in fiscal 1995.
At a briefing to unveil its annual report, IFC Executive Vice President Jannik Lindbaek told reporters he expected total financing this year would be up 8 percent to 10 percent.

This was somewhat slower than in recent years, he said, noting that over the past five years total financing by the agency has doubled as countries around the world rushed to embrace the free enterprise system.

"We see that in some of our important countries, alternative sources of financing have become available, so we are less important to some of these countries," he said. "We're talking about Eastern Europe and some parts of Asia."

At the same time, he said the IFC was launching a new initiative to expand its activities in smaller and poorer nations, targeting some 16 countries it said were undergoing particularly difficult transitions to market economies.
They included Bosnia and Herzegovina, Cambodia, countries in the Eastern Caribbean, Central Africa, as well as the Slovak Republic and the West Bank and Gaza.

But the IFC made clear that it was working to ensure that it did not get into the way of private capital moving into developing country markets, consulting extensively with the private sector to reduce investment conflicts.

This was good news at the Institute of International Finance, which separately reported its annual forecast showing that net private investment in the major emerging markets will reach a record $225 billion this year, up from $208 billion in 1995.

The group, which provides economic analysis for commercial banks and other financial institutions, said it was critical that the International Monetary Fund and World Bank work closely with the private sector so they don't get in each other's way.

Moreover, IIF Managing Director Charles Dallara said it might be better for the international financial institutions to walk more softly during crisis rather than mobilise huge bailouts as was done for Mexico at the start of last year.
The new information on global investment comes in conjunction with the annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank, which begins next week.
